topic: std::bitset Conversion to Integral Types and Overflow Exception
explanation:
The `std::bitset` provides member functions `to_ulong()` and `to_ullong()` to convert the stored binary pattern into standard unsigned integer types (`unsigned long` and `unsigned long long`, respectively).

Purpose: This allows direct arithmetic manipulation of the bit pattern as a standard numeric type.

Technical Details:
- `to_ulong()`: Returns the integral value, provided the bitset size (N) is less than or equal to the number of bits in `unsigned long` (typically 32 or 64).
- `to_ullong()`: Used for bitsets potentially larger than `unsigned long`, up to the size of `unsigned long long` (typically 64 bits).
- **Exception Guarantee**: If the value represented by the bitset is too large to fit into the target integral type (i.e., if any bit position $i \ge \text{sizeof}(\text{Target Type}) \times 8$ is set), the function throws an `std::overflow_error` exception.
- Complexity: Generally O(N), where N is the compile-time size of the bitset.

Pitfalls: Failure to handle the `std::overflow_error` when converting large bitsets results in program termination. Developers must ensure that the size N of the bitset is compatible with the target type or implement robust exception handling.
practical_example: When implementing custom serialization or deserialization routines that read fixed-width binary data (e.g., network packet headers) into a `bitset`, the application must check the size of the packet fields against the available integral types before calling `to_ulong()`. If a 40-bit field is read, conversion to a standard 32-bit `unsigned long` must be protected by exception handling.
